"It's Ma's kitchen too." Tanuja kept rolling rotis.
"I'm sorry about your engagement. I promised I'd come, and I stayed for the client call."
"You chose work. Like always."
"I did. It was wrong." Nikita picked up the second rolling pin. "When I'm seventy, I want to say I kept my word to the people I love. I can't fix that day. But I don't want to be the sister who keeps choosing the call."
Tanuja flipped a roti. "So what now?"
"Now I show up. Sunday lunches. And for your wedding I've taken the whole week off. It's already approved."
"And if you mess up again?"
"I probably will, somewhere. Then I'll say sorry again."
Tanuja pushed the dough bowl toward her. "At least make them round."

qa.a: Nikita may be hoping to show, not just say, that she will show up now, by working beside Tanuja in Ma's kitchen.

passage: Last spring I nearly took the job that paid double. I, Sahil, a man who'd always said the fisheries project mattered, kept the offer letter open for three days. What stopped me was a question Dolma asked over momos: "When you're old, what do you want to look back and say?" I thought of the fishermen's cooperative whose data system I had promised to finish. So I stayed until it was done, then switched jobs in autumn with a proper handover. I also finally called my cousin after two years of silence over a stupid property argument. It was stiff. It's better now. I still carry regrets. I missed my friend's farewell for a deadline, and I can't undo that. No life comes out clean. But I want mine to be one I can tell without flinching.

Sunday night
Tired enough to cancel Nirmala's driving lesson this morning. Didn't. I promised her in March, and she has been practising gear changes on a broom handle. She stalled eleven times, then drove to the gurdwara corner and back, grinning.
Lately I ask myself one question on the metro: when I'm eighty, what do I hope I can say about my life? Not "I had the best appraisal." Something like: I kept my word. I made up with people. My work helped someone.
So this week: drove with Nirmala. Called Bhaji after eight months of silence over the house; we didn't solve it, but we talked for twenty minutes. Said yes to the flood-mapping project at work, though it pays nothing extra.
I still have regrets. I didn't visit Nani enough before she died, and I'll carry that. But I can choose what comes next.
Gurpreet

qa.q: What had Nirmala been practising gear changes on?
qa.a: She had been practising on a broom handle.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet hope to say at eighty?
qa.a: Gurpreet wants to say 'I kept my word, I made up with people, my work helped someone', not just 'I had the best appraisal'.

qa.q: Which ordinary choices this week show Gurpreet's question at work?
qa.a: Keeping the driving promise while tired, calling Bhaji after eight months, and taking on the unpaid flood-mapping project.

qa.q: What might the call mean to Bhaji, even though the house issue wasn't solved?
qa.a: It may show him that Gurpreet values the relationship more than winning the argument, opening a way back after eight months of silence.
